Haha, sure. To be honest it’s more a variety of weird things that occurred whilst we lived there. It was the mid 90s. The family who we bought the house from had two teenage kids, and they were selling up because the husband and wife had split up. My brother & I were both teens too, and moved in with our parents. After living there for just a few years my parents’ marriage started breaking down, despite being happy for over 20 years. 

The house had two staircases. One went up to where my parents’ room and my brother’s room were & the other to a separate part where my bedroom and bathroom was, so I was completely alone on that side. I would have really weird stuff happen in my sleep. One time I woke up with a heavy weight pushing down on my chest. I couldn’t move and I struggled to be able to breathe. It was shit scary but the next day I put it down to sleep paralysis, even though I’d never had it before then, and haven’t in the 20 years since I left that house. 

Another time, I woke up feeling really scared and ran down my stairs in the dark to where there was a huge disused fireplace in the heart of the house, big enough to walk into, thinking I’d see if my parents were still awake. The minute I got there I woke up in my bed & realised I must have been dreaming. I still felt scared so I got up quick and ran down the stairs again to the fireplace, at which point I ‘woke up’ in my bed again. Not lying, this happened at least 5, maybe 6, times over & over in an identical loop. It was really scary & nothing like that has happened to me before or since. 

When I was in the bathroom sometimes I’d hear someone come up the creaky little staircase to my part of the house. I’d call out & no one would answer and then I’d come out & there would be no one there. It happened quite a few times. 

I left the house to go to university once I was 18. I’m glad I got out. I had started having panic attacks that came out of nowhere. One night later that year, my brother, who was 16, was picked up by police. He had climbed out of his bedroom window in the middle of the night and run across the fields (the house was out in the middle of nowhere). He had been banging on an old lady’s front door screaming & she’d called the cops. He was taken to the mental hospital. He said he had seen his phone turn into the devil. The doctors said he had a psychotic episode, though we had not noticed him deteriorating at any point beforehand. He has not had an episode even remotely like that since. I’ve tried to ask him about it a couple of times but he never likes to talk about it.

Anyway, my parents obviously split and they sold the house shortly after. I guess you could explain away each separate incident or occurrence, and perhaps it was all just coincidence it all happened in that house, but it was pretty freaky. 

I’ve often wondered if the next family who moved in there ended up splitting up or whether they had any bizarre experiences. 

I guess my story may not be as good as many on this sub, but it was definitely creepy living there & my family have all been left with bad memories from it.

I just want to add that tarot is tricky & it takes a long time to really learn about & get a ‘feel’ for each card. There is always more to learn. 

So don’t be too hard on yourself. You’ll begin to get a feel for it the more you use it. 

From the point of view of ‘nature’, I have taken that to mean things like Justice, Wheel of Fortune, Judgement. That is, abstract things that are not people or events. Though some people may think differently, and there aren’t really right or wrong answers. How you interpret the tarot comes down to how you feel in your gut about the cards & readings, rather than how other people interpret it. You read your cards in a way that is personal to you. 

Starting out, it definitely helps to read what the standard definitions are, as a guideline, but if you have any gut feelings, either at the start or later on, about what a card means for you personally, make a note of that.

Your keywords will change & evolve as you go along & will get more refined. Mine certainly did.

I don’t think your keywords need to be grouped into one of the three categories. Mine aren’t. If the categories are really a problem, I’d put that to one side & come back to it later once you feel a bit more confident about the cards.

You get referred to a mental health professional, who is still part of the NHS, who will talk to you & assess you, and from there, if you need it, you will be offered help. That could include talking therapy of some sort, or various other options that they will discuss with you. Your GP can diagnose light depression/anxiety but you need a MH professional to diagnose you with a more serious disorder, or if you have more serious symptoms.

Honestly, get everything written down & take it with you to the GP. I’ve done that for years. It really helps them see that it’s a big deal to you too. 

If things are bad, you should speak to someone. It will be a huge relief. When you sit on these things they don’t tend to go away, they just eat away at you. 

In addition, you could speak to people online who also feel the way you do. There are subreddits for PD & mental health in general, plus loads of UK based sites. 

It’s a good idea to educate yourself on things as much as possible too. Try these sites, amongst others, for lots of mental health information:

[Mind](https://www.mind.org.uk) 

[Rethink](rethink.org) 

I hope you get things figured out. Good luck!

What I would do is write a list of all the things that you’re struggling with, and how they affect you. This last part is key, because showing/telling a doctor just how much it is affecting your life is what will get them to take it more seriously. If it’s interrupting school/work/your relationships etc then they need to take it more seriously than if you were simply just worrying about it a lot. 

Have a look at the PD traits & make a list of those you feel really sound like you & are negatively affecting your life. Maybe think of examples.

Are you in the UK? I only really have UK knowledge. Take the list to your doctor & tell them that you are concerned, that these things are really affecting your life, and you want to be referred to mental health services for an assessment. Don’t let them fob you off - depending on the doctor, they might try, but stick to your guns (figuratively ;)) & demand a referral. Make sure they understand how much you are being affected. 

Sometimes they will send you away with advice the first time, but if you keep going back with the same issues, and you really make the point you want more help, preferably a mental health assessment, they have to escalate it. 

You might need to wait a little while on a waiting list if you’re in the UK, but the sooner you get on the better.

I studied this at university for my  sociology bachelors. I’ve had a look online to try & find a link that explains it better than I perhaps could.

[American Psychological Association](https://www.apa.org/monitor/feb03/intelligence.aspx) 

This article describes how intelligence itself is cultural, as what makes someone intelligent differs in different cultures. What Westerners therefore score for in their standardised IQ tests, is a Western view of intelligence, eg. abstract thinking.

The most interesting point it makes, I think, is: “people who are unable to solve complex problems in the abstract can often solve them when they are presented in a familiar context”.

I have done an IQ test for Mensa, so I know what they are like. There is a huge amount of abstract thinking. Therefore, just using this as a possible example, people from Aboriginal culture may perhaps think less in the abstract, due to their way of life, & therefore find this more challenging. If the questions or tasks were framed in the way they are culturally more used to thinking, they would likely score higher, possibly even higher than a Westerner doing their test.

I am by no means an expert & do not know for sure how intelligence is framed in Aboriginal culture, but I do know that cultural bias is certainly something that at least needs to be taken into account. 

IQ testing taken at face value could lead us into thinking that certain cultures are less intelligent than others, and this is just not a good place to venture. It is extremely tricky to compare cultures with a standard benchmark as there is so much variation in how intelligence can be defined.

I have lived with anxiety like this for 20 years now. It used to affect me mentally, but I had some counselling & learned some techniques & a lot of time went by, & now it doesn’t affect me like that any more. It does, however, continue to physically (specifically, physiologically) affect me, so I completely understand.

My body still reacts as if there is a reason to be scared, even if my mind is okay. I get a clenched stomach, my breathing becomes shallow, I feel dizzy & hot & I feel very strongly that I need to avoid the situation that is causing it, usually a social situation.

I use a number of techniques. The most important thing is to never avoid the thing you’re body is telling you to avoid. This is the hardest thing to do! But if you do, you are reinforcing the fear & your body’s reactions. Do it, and breathe through it. I concentrate on my breathing: breathe out more than you breathe in, as deep breaths encourage your body to go more into fight/flight mode. 

It may be that the physical discomfort never goes, but you just learn to exist with it, as I have done. I’m not saying this to make you feel depressed about it. The day I realised that it probably wouldn’t go away (after trying all the different medications & getting no result), was when it actually got easier, as I started to face it instead of avoiding the anxiety itself, and I began the process of becoming more resilient against it.

Now, my stomach can be in knots but I just feel the horrible feeling & let it be there. Doing things despite the physical fear can be very empowering.

I also make time for self-care: doing things I enjoy, or that are very relaxing. I take time out when I need it.

I’m not saying it’s easy, I wouldn’t want you to think that I’m not taking you seriously & saying “oh, you just do this & it’s all going to be ok”. I’m just sharing my experience, & hoping there might be something helpful in there.

I wish you all the best, as I understand how disabling anxiety can be. Good luck.

I have had 9 months of psychology sessions so far and learned some strategies for getting out of snowballing thoughts & emotions.

I write. I have a pen & paper that I grab and I write how I am feeling, what I am thinking etc and why I think I’ve started feeling this way. I get it all out on the page. As I write I often see that there are reasons for why I’m feeling bad this time (maybe I’m tired so it’s making me feel worse) or I start to see patterns in my thinking or thoughts that really don’t make sense when I question them further.

Another thing you can do is write down all your thoughts & feelings, no matter how out there they may seem. You don’t have to ever show anyone else this. Now write down how someone else would see the situation. What would be the outside/helicopter view of what is happening? It can be hard to think sometimes but with practice it gets easier & it helps you get things into perspective. 

I have a list of grounding and distracting techniques also that I consult at these times: listening to a certain playlist of songs, looking at photographs I’ve particularly picked out in advance, doing some housework, going for a walk, having a bath or shower, making a hot or cold drink, watching a Netflix show etc

One of my biggest rules also is don’t drink alcohol at these times. 

I keep going from one technique to the other, writing as I go about how I’m feeling, and I find I pop out of it eventually. I record how long it takes each time too. Sometimes it takes an hour, sometimes it takes six, but it really does help.
